paragraphs: (a) In the Mishnah: Avot 2:1, 4:20; Sheviit 6:4; Maaserot 5:5; Bikkurim 1:11; Shabbat 6:5, 12:3; Ketubot 2:4; Nedarim 3:11; Nazir 1:4, 4:5; Sotah 3:5, 5:1, 9:15; Gittin 5:6; Bava Kamma, source פיה, 3 [chapter label unclear]; Makkot 1:8, 2:1; Avodah Zarah 2:6, 4:5, 5:11; Menachot 6:3, 8:6, 13:2, 5, 8, 9; Chullin 3:4; Bekhorot 7:6; Arakhin 4:2, 8:5, 9:3, 8; Temurah 4:3, 6:2; Meilah 5:3; Middot 3:4; Ohalot 18:9.

(b) He is called the unqualified Rabbi. Chapter 3 of Kiddushin; Jerusalem Talmud, end of chapter 1 of Peah: Rabbi and R. Yehudah HaNasi disagree. Let someone of broad understanding correct this, for one cannot say that R. Yehudah HaNasi means his grandson R. Yehudah Nesia; see Berabbi above. I later found in Sedeh Yehoshua: “Apparently the name of R. Yehudah HaNasi's disputant is missing. One cannot say Rabbi is our holy Rabbi and R. Yehudah HaNasi his grandson R. Yehudah Nesia, for the latter was not our holy Rabbi's disputant. Alternatively, read Berabbi instead of Rabbi: a sage named Berabbi.” He is called our holy Rabbi. They asked Rabbi why he was called our holy Rabbi. He answered, “I have never looked at my circumcision”: Shabbat 118b; Jerusalem Talmud, end of Sanhedrin, Chelek, halakhah 6, and Megillah, chapter 3, halakhah 2. He never put his hand below his belt—Shabbat there—even though married: Tosafot, Kol HaYad. Arukh, entry Ammato, says his hands were clothed in thick cloth; see Kohelet Rabbah 9. Alternatively, “holy” follows the Jerusalem Talmud: circumcision was prohibited, and his father sanctified him to Heaven and circumcised him. Livnat HaSappir likewise writes this. So it appears, since Rabbi was born on the day R. Akiva died, and R. Akiva was killed during the persecution. Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 10b: the king's wife loved Rabbi's mother. His mother exchanged him for Antoninus and nursed Antoninus, while the king's wife nursed Rabbi. They brought him before the king, found him uncircumcised, and released him in peace. Thus Antoninus converted because Rabbi's mother nursed him. See part 1, year 3900. The work abbreviated ג״נ, letter resh, writes concerning Bameh Ishah: a woman died leaving an infant to nurse. Two breasts like a woman's opened on the father, and he nursed his son. The king's wife, for nursing Rabbi, was reincarnated in this man to merit the world to come. Abaye expounds, “How inferior this man is”: his poverty contrasts with her former place in a king's palace. He is called Rabbi Rabbah. Jerusalem Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, halakhah 9: R. Yehudah HaNasi is called “our teachers” in three places, concerning bills of divorce, oil, and the sandal, and is called “the court that permitted oil.” The Babylonian Talmud implies that this was his grandson R. Yehudah Nesia; see there.

(c) He was the son of R. Shimon ben Gamliel of Yavneh, descended from Hillel (see there), of David's seed on his father's side and Benjamin on his mother's. Bameh Behemah, Shabbat 56a: Rabbi, who descends from David, turns and expounds in David's favor. As Moses was seventh from Abraham, Rabbi was seventh from Hillel, like the western lamp, and holy like the Sabbath: Hillel; his son Shimon; his son R. N. the Elder [ר״נ; probably a letter-slip for ר״ג, Rabban Gamliel the Elder]; his son R. Shimon, who was killed; his son Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh; his son R. Shimon; his son Rabbi. See Rambam's introduction to his commentary on Mishnah Yevamot. What is written there in the name of the great teacher Shmuel ben Chofni contains scribal errors and omissions; Sefer Yuchasin, 158a, likewise has omissions. Mishnat Chakhamim, section 640, also requires correction. He was the twelfth generation of tannaim: Shimon HaTzadik; Antigonos; Yosi ben Yoezer; Yehoshua ben Perachyah; Shimon ben Shetach; Shemayah; Hillel, etc. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi form another generation, corresponding to twelve tribes, stars, zodiacal signs, and “ve-tarshim” [ותרשים, unresolved]. Alternatively: seven generations to Hillel, then Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, R. Eliezer, R. Akiva, R. Shimon and R. Meir, and Rabbi: twelve. He is the thirty-fifth recipient; according to Rambam, the thirty-fourth. From Hillel the Elder through Hillel son of R. Yehudah Nesia son of R. Gamliel son of our holy Rabbi are ten generations: Yuchasin, sequence of generations under Rabbi. Megalleh Amukkot, section 246: forty generations from Moses to Rabbi; according to Rambam, forty from Moses to Rav Ashi.

(d) He made the mishnayot and signed his name at the beginning of his work: me-eimatai has the numerical value of “I am Yehudah, holy.” So the introduction to Beer Avraham writes in the name of Megalleh Amukkot's author. Yet how could someone as humble as he call himself “Yehudah, holy”? Arukh writes that it should read mi-matai. But the alef need not be counted, since with the inclusive unit the number agrees. R. Yitzchak Luria writes that me-eimatai denotes awe and fear: we recite the Shema to protect against fear of harmful spirits; its numerical value is 501. See my book on numbers, where you will find an explanation of this. At the beginning of HaGozel, Rabbenu Tam says the mishnayot existed before Rabbi, who arranged them, while the baraitot taught by his student R. Chiyya were what Rabbi added to the mishnayot. End of quotation. See there and R. Oshaya. He spread Torah in Israel. Seeing the long exile and prevalent forgetfulness, he said, “It is time to act for the Lord,” although “they have annulled Your Torah,” since writing the Oral Torah is forbidden. He was a tanna [source חנא]: Taanit 14b, Rabbi is a tanna and may disagree; also an amora, see part 1 above in the generational sequence. Avodah Zarah, chapter 5, uses “It was stated: Rabbi and R. Chiyya,” rather than “It was taught” or “The rabbis taught” [source ולרי is defective]. Pesachim, chapter 1, 13a: “Whose view does this teaching of Rabbi follow?” The term shemaata is particular to amoraim. Bava Kamma 116a: Rav objected to Rabbi, a formulation used of one amora addressing another. After the tannaim's words were closed and the great men died, Rabbi, R. Chiyya, and Rav remained on the level of amoraim. Responsa Halakhot Ketannot, 2:71 [received locator מ״ט]: our holy Rabbi is a tanna but is sometimes counted as an amora, because he was the end of the tannaim and beginning of the amoraim. In Rabbi's time they had respite from persecution. Rabbi grew up with Antoninus because of the circumcision decree, and there was relief and rescue. The sages, his father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's colleagues, saw fit to arrange laws and rulings and establish anonymous texts. It was called by Rabbi's name, though he was young and like a student before his teacher: first, because he was nasi, son of presidents; second, because all were saved through him. At that time they were called tannaim, meaning repeaters and teachers. Thus after the elders' closure of Mishnah and baraita, Rabbi and his sons and R. Chiyya and his sons remained among the beginning amoraim, although appearing in Mishnah and baraita. R. Yehoshua ben Levi's words were likewise fixed at the Mishnah's end although he was an amora. End of quotation. See R. Yehudah Nesia and R. Gamliel son of Rabbi above. Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, section 16: Rabbi was the end of the tannaim, with R. Natan. The work ג״נ, letter kaf, writes: Methuselah is our holy Rabbi, since he studied six hundred orders of Mishnah, while Rabbi wrote six orders, each encompassing one hundred. Letter pe says R. Pinchas ben Yair, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and our holy Rabbi are one spark.

(e) Rabbi honored wealthy men: Eruvin 86a. He maintained most students, as in Eruvin 53b, “Let the eagles fly to their nests”: R. Shimshon, end of Terumot, mishnah 9. Rabbi's stable-master was wealthier than King Shapur: Shabbat 113b; Bava Metzia 85a. From Moses until Rabbi, Torah and greatness were not found together in one place: Gittin 59a; Sanhedrin 36a. He opened his storehouses in drought years; see Yonatan ben Uzziel.

(f) Antoninus, king of Rome, was Rabbi's friend, and Rabbi secretly converted him. He sent Rabbi broken gold in sacks with wheat on top. He went daily to Rabbi through a cave; see R. Yosi ben Kisma. He served Rabbi and bent down before him so Rabbi could stand on him when mounting his bed. He died before Rabbi, who said, “The bond has separated”: Avodah Zarah, chapter 1, 10b; see there at length. Kohelet Rabbah, on “There is an evil I saw under the sun,” says Rabbi died before Antoninus the Younger, grandson of Antoninus the Elder. Antoninus asked Rabbi several matters: Chelek, Sanhedrin 91. He sent Rabbi asking how to replenish his depleted treasuries: Bereshit Rabbah, section 67; asked Rabbi, “What does the verse mean, etc.?”—beginning of section 84; and asked Rabbi to pray for him—Vayikra Rabbah, section 16. When Rabbi went to the government, he studied this passage: Bereshit Rabbah, section 78. Antoninus made Rabbi a feast: Esther Midrash. Rabbi made him a Sabbath feast: Bereshit Rabbah, section 11. Justina, daughter of Severus son of Antoninus, asked Rabbi, “At what age does a woman marry?”: Niddah 45a. Three emperors lived in his days: Antoninus, then Marcus Antoninus, then Commodus. All persecuted Christians, showed favor to our holy Rabbi, and honored him: Tzemach David. Megalleh Amukkot, section 84: Yehudah HaNasi forms the initials “he was a spark of Jacob our father”; Antoninus was a spark and reincarnation of Esau. Artaban sent Rabbi pearls: Bereshit Rabbah, section 35.

(g) Rabbi was with seventy members of the Sanhedrin at Beit Shearim, Tiberias, and Tzippori. Tiberias was lowest of all, and the Sanhedrin went there in its tenth exile. See Rabban Gamliel the Elder above; Yuchasin under Shmuel the Younger. His residence was at Beit Shearim: Sanhedrin 32b; end of HaNose in Ketubot. Also Tiberias, as in Megillah, chapter 1. When he fell ill, they took him to Tzippori, whose elevation and air were pleasant. He was in Tzippori seventeen years and applied to himself, “Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years”: Bereshit Rabbah, section 96. After his death they took him to Beit Shearim through the towns in his honor: Nigmar HaDin.

(h) His colleague was R. Elazar son of R. Shimon. After R. Elazar died, Rabbi sought to marry his wife. She refused, saying, “Shall a vessel used by the holy be used by the ordinary?” Jerusalem Talmud, HaMatznia, halakhah 5: there they say, “Where the master of the house hung his weapons, shall the shepherd's dog hang its basket?” He sent her, “Granted that he was greater than I in Torah, but who is greater than I in good deeds?” She said, “I do not know that he was greater than you in Torah”—your own mouth testified against you—“but I know it concerning good deeds, since he accepted sufferings, etc.” Rabbi said, “Sufferings are dear.” He accepted them for thirteen years: six with tzemirta and seven with tzefidna; some say the reverse. They came through an incident and departed through an incident; see there. Throughout Rabbi's years of suffering, the world did not need rain: Bava Metzia 84–85. When he entered the privy, he cried out, and his voice surpassed the mules' voices, so that seafarers heard it. He suffered from his eye, and Shmuel was his physician; there.

(i) Elijah regularly attended his academy. Once, on the New Moon, Elijah came late. He asked why. Elijah answered, “I had to wake Abraham, wash his hands, let him pray, and lay him down; likewise Isaac and Jacob. I do not wake all three together, lest they overpower through mercy and bring the Messiah before his time.” He asked whether their like existed in this world. He answered, “R. Chiyya and his sons”; see there, Bava Metzia there. Nedarim 41a: Rabbi knew thirteen aspects of the law. He taught R. Chiyya seven. Rabbi fell ill and forgot them; R. Chiyya reminded him, but six were lost. A launderer taught R. Chiyya, and R. Chiyya taught Rabbi; see there. Rabbi told R. Chiyya, “Go to Ein Tav to sanctify the month.” Rashi explains: to prevent murmuring, because they had seen the old moon all the twenty-ninth day. My teacher explained that persecution had been decreed in his locality, forbidding sanctification of the month: Rosh Hashanah 25a. This requires investigation, since all the emperors favored Rabbi throughout his days; see R. Elazar ben Shamua. Moed Katan 16: Rabbi decreed that students not be taught in the marketplace. R. Chiyya went and taught his two nephews, Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chana, there. Rabbi was angry. R. Chiyya came to visit him, and he said, “Ayya, who is calling you outside?” Knowing he held a grievance, he observed a reprimand for thirty days. On the thirtieth day he sent, “Come, etc.” He asked why he had done this. He answered, “It is written, ‘Wisdom cries aloud outside.’” He replied, “If you have read, you have not studied, etc. ‘Wisdom outside’ is as Rava said: whoever studies inside, Torah proclaims him outside, etc.” The words “as Rava said” were not Rabbi's: Rav Yehudah was born on the day Rabbi died, and Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died. Rather, Rabbi said simply, “Whoever studies inside, etc.” The arranger, in closing the Gemara, said “as Rava said,” since Rava's exposition was then well known. See the general rules.

(j) The seven qualities enumerated by the sages were fulfilled in Rabbi and his sons: Avot, chapter 6; see R. Shimon ben Menasya. Jerusalem Kilayim; Bereshit Rabbah, section 33; Ketubot; HaPoalim: he was exceedingly humble and said, “Whatever they tell me, I do, except what the elders of Beteira did for my ancestor Hillel”; see there and R. Yehudah ben Beteira. “If Rav Huna the exilarch came up, I would seat him above myself”; see there. R. Chiyya told him, “Rav Huna the exilarch is outside.” Rabbi's face changed color; see there. R. Chiyya observed a reprimand for thirty days: Rav Sherira Gaon in Yuchasin. Sanhedrin, chapter 1: Rabbi once went somewhere and saw an error caused by a student's exposition that “water of marshes does not render food susceptible,” when it should have been “water of eggs.” He decreed that a student not rule without authorization, and authorized Rabbah bar bar Chana and Rav; see there. He made his students a meal of soft and hard tongues: Vayikra Rabbah, beginning of section 33. He was always saddened and worried by Israel's exile. To cheer him, Levi demonstrated a kiddah bow (see there), as did R. Chiyya (see there); Bar Kappara was humorous and cheered him; see there. HaNoder, Nedarim 50b: on a day Rabbi laughed, calamity came to the world. When he passed his hands over his eyes, he accepted the yoke of Heaven's kingship: Berakhot 13b. His daughter died at Beit Shearim, yet he did not refrain from expounding all day. Elisha Acher's daughter came before him; see there. One who sees Rabbi in a dream may expect wisdom: Berakhot 57b. His son Yavetz entered the Garden of Eden alive; see there.

(k) Rabbi asked R. Yehoshua ben Korcha how he had attained long life. Rabbi said to him, “My teacher, bless me.” He blessed him to attain half his days; see there. Rabbi lived one hundred years; see part 1, year 3979. He was born on the day R. Akiva died, and became nasi at thirty, in 3815 [as printed. Part 1 gives 3910 at age thirty and cites an alternative of 3920.]. R. Meir was tall in his generation; Rabbi reached his shoulder, and Rav reached Rabbi's shoulder: Bemidbar Rabbah, section 9. Niddah 24b: Rabbi was tall in his generation, and R. Chiyya reached his shoulder; see Abba Shaul.

(l) Ketubot 103a: at his death he told his sons, “Take care to honor your mother”—their stepmother. “Let a lamp burn in its place, a table be set, and a bed spread in its place, etc.” He came home every Sabbath eve. Once a neighbor came calling at the door. His maidservant said, “Be quiet: Rabbi is sitting here.” He no longer came, so as not to cast aspersions on earlier righteous men, lest people say they were not righteous because they had not been allowed to come home like Rabbi. “Yosef Chofni and Shimon Efrati served me in life and will serve me in death.” They thought he meant this world; seeing their biers precede his, they said he meant the other world, etc. He also prophesied, “Today Rav Adda bar Ahavah will sit in Abraham's bosom”; see there. Kiddushin 72 has many prophecies Rabbi spoke. He said, “I need Israel's sages.” They entered. He told them, “Do not eulogize me in the small towns; convene the academy after thirty days,” rather than being occupied with eulogy. “Although my son Shimon is wise, my son Gamliel is nasi,” for he filled his ancestors' place in fear of sin. “Chanina bar Chama shall preside over the academy.” He entrusted the orders of wisdom to his younger son R. Shimon, and the orders of presidency to his elder son R. Gamliel. He told him, “Conduct your presidency loftily”—see Rashi's three explanations—“cast awe upon the students.” He commanded three things before his death: Bereshit Rabbah, section 96. He wept over Torah and commandments. He suffered intestinal illness with diarrhea, because those with intestinal illness retain their understanding until death. Rashi, Kol Kitvei, explains that they suffer and their sins are purged. The Jerusalem Talmud likewise says the earlier pious men suffered intestinal illness for ten or twenty days before death, to purge sins and come innocent to the world to come. Tosafot, Kol Kitvei, writes: to purge food and drink, to be clean and pure. See Semachot, chapter 3. Tosafot, HaNose there, writes that although those with intestinal illness are exempt from phylacteries, Rabbi conducted himself with exceptional holiness and knew well how to take care. On the day he died, the rabbis decreed a fast and prayed, saying, “Whoever says Rabbi has died shall be stabbed with a sword.” Rabbi's maidservant went onto the roof and said, “Those above seek Rabbi, and those below seek Rabbi. May those below prevail over those above.” Seeing how often he entered the privy, removed and replaced his phylacteries, and suffered, she said, “May those above prevail over those below.” The rabbis would not cease praying. She took a jar and threw it from the roof. They fell silent, and Rabbi died. Chesed LeAvraham, spring 5, end of river 25: that maidservant of Rabbi's house was of the mystery of the maidservants at the sea, whose standing was greater than the sages'. Therefore the rabbis observed the ban she imposed on that man and learned several things from them. The writings of R. Yitzchak Luria likewise say Rabbi's maidservants, often mentioned in the Talmud, especially Moed Katan 17a, from whom many things were learned, were those of whom the sages said, “A maidservant saw at the sea what Ezekiel did not see.” The rabbis told Bar Kappara to go investigate. He found Rabbi had died, tore his clothing, turned the tear behind him, and began: “Angels and pillars grasped the holy ark; the angels overcame the pillars”—the righteous men. At death Rabbi raised his ten fingers toward heaven and said, “Master of the universe, it is revealed and known before You that I labored with my ten fingers in Torah, yet did not enjoy even with a little finger.” Berakhot 57b and Avodah Zarah, chapter 1, 11a, say radish and lettuce never ceased from his table. Tosafot explains: for his household. Tzeror HaChayyim writes that this alludes to revealed and concealed learning; see there. “May there be peace in my rest.” A heavenly voice said, “Let him come in peace; they shall rest on their beds.” On the day Rabbi died, a heavenly voice said all present at his death were destined for life in the world to come. A launderer came before him every day, but did not come that day. Hearing this, he climbed to the roof, fell to the ground, and died. A heavenly voice said that launderer too was destined for life in the world to come. See Maharit on Ketubot concerning how he injured himself. The work ג״נ says the launderer was Laban, for a launderer whitens garments, while Rabbi was in Abraham's mystery; there was his repair. He died on Sabbath eve. Miracles occurred that day: all the towns assembled to eulogize him. They brought him through eighteen synagogues and took him down to Beit Sherai. Daylight remained until everyone reached home, filled a barrel of water, and lit a lamp. When the sun set, the rooster crowed. They became distressed, saying perhaps they had violated the Sabbath. A heavenly voice said, “Whoever did not neglect Rabbi's eulogy is assured life in the world to come, except the launderer.” Hearing this, he climbed to the roof, threw himself down, and died. A heavenly voice said, “Even the launderer”: Jerusalem Kilayim 9:4; Ketubot, HaNose. “On the day Rabbi died, holiness ceased.” Tosafot there says he was called our holy Rabbi, as at the end of Sotah 49: when Rabbi died, humility and fear ceased, holiness included. R. Chayyim the priest said, “Had I been present when Rabbenu Tam died, I would have become impure for him,” since “holiness ceased” here means priestly holiness. Jerusalem Talmud, Mi SheMetu, mishnah 1, and beginning of chapter 7 of Nazir, explicitly asks whether a priest may become impure for a nasi. When R. Yehudah Nesia died, R. Yannai proclaimed, “There is no priesthood today.” This does not appear correct to Rabbi [the cited commentator], who thinks that passage concerns a beit peras, a field of doubtful grave impurity. See Maharit on Ketubot 103, who writes that it concerns definite impurity. Ran says that because everyone owes a nasi honor, even a priest may attend his burial, as with an unattended corpse. [The received text cites Ein Bein HaMuddar. The explanation appears in Ran on Rif Ketubot 61b, HaNose.] Rambam and Tur likewise write this. I wonder what was novel for Rabbi beyond all presidents. The work abbreviated נא״י writes that our holy Rabbi is buried at Tzippori, with the monument opposite the cave's entrance and a stone door; see R. Chiyya. His wife and sons are buried there. A pleasant fragrance from his grave is smelled for a parasang and more. There is a spring of living water, running forcefully throughout the week, but not flowing even a drop on the Sabbath. R. Shimon and Rabban Gamliel are in a cave beside the village. On the day Rabbi died, Rav Yehudah was born in Babylonia; see there.

(m) Rabbi's teachers: his father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; R. Yaakov ben Korshai (see there); and R. Akiva's five students whom R. Yehudah ben Bava ordained; see there. Perhaps the unqualified R. Yaakov in the Mishnah was his teacher, rather than R. Yaakov, R. Elazar's father (see there), or R. Yaakov, Elisha's daughter's son, or R. Yaakov Chatya in Chagigah. Yoma 61a, near the end: Rabbi said, “R. Yaakov taught me.” Gittin 14b: R. Yehudah HaNasi said in R. Yaakov's name, who said in R. Meir's name. The five are: (1) R. Shimon—Shabbat 147b; Eruvin 91a; Menachot 72a, near the end; Rashi, Shabbat 32b and Beitzah 26a, near the end, Rabbi was R. Shimon's student. See Jerusalem Talmud, HaMatznia, and Tosafot, Makkot 9b: Rabbi said, “When I went to study Torah with R. Shimon at Tekoa.” (2) R. Elazar ben Shamua, Yom HaKippurim; see there. (3) R. Yehudah bar Ilai; see there. (4) R. Meir, from whom he received all the Mishnah. Eruvin 13b: Rav—Abba Arikha, see there—said, “I am sharper than my colleagues because I saw R. Meir from behind.” Tosafot, Menachot 104a, says some read Rabbi because of Jerusalem Beitzah, Mashilin, halakhah 2: Rabbi merited Torah because he saw R. Meir at his son R. Shimon's wedding. They were clapping the backs of their hands on the Sabbath. R. Meir passed, heard them, and said, “Have our teachers permitted the Sabbath?” Rabbi heard him and asked, “Who has come to chastise us inside our house?” R. Meir heard Rabbi's voice and fled. They followed. The wind blew his wrap off his neck; Rabbi looked from his window and saw R. Meir's neck from behind. He said, “I merited Torah only because I saw R. Meir's neck from behind.” Rashi in Eruvin explains that he sat behind him in the academy. “Had I seen him from the front, I would have been sharper still,” for it is written, “Your eyes shall see your teachers.” Jerusalem Talmud: R. Shimon son of Rabbi was eating in the marketplace. R. Meir saw and said, “It is no credit to a Torah scholar to do so.” This is difficult: R. Meir died before R. Yosi and R. Yehudah; see there. R. Yehudah did not want to admit Sumkhos, R. Meir's student, to the study house after R. Meir died; see there. How, then, could he attend R. Shimon son of Rabbi's wedding? I have heard it said that this was an angel in R. Meir's likeness. Yet Tosafot, Menachot 104a, beginning, says R. Yehudah lived in Rabbi's days, since even R. Meir, who died before R. Yehudah, attended R. Shimon son of Rabbi's wedding. End of quotation. See R. Yehudah bar Ilai above. (5) R. Yosi ben Chalafta; see there. He was subordinate before Rabbi. Perhaps because they were his teachers, he gave their names without qualification in the Mishnah, out of honor: he did not name their fathers, such as R. Shimon ben Yochai or R. Yehudah bar Ilai, so as to name his teacher only indirectly. Yuchasin, in the sequence of tannaim under R. Yehoshua ben Korcha, says R. Yehoshua ben Korcha was Rabbi's teacher; we likewise find Rabbi telling him, “My teacher, bless me,” above. Yet Yuchasin at its end calls him Rabbi's colleague. Tosafot, Menachot 38b, says R. Yosi HaGelili was Rabbi's teacher. This requires investigation by the generational sequence: R. Yehudah, R. Yosi HaGelili's student, was Rabbi's teacher, and R. Chanina, R. Yosi HaGelili's son, sat in the court of Rabbi's father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. But he lived long: R. Meir's wife called him “foolish Galilean.” Thus he was both R. Yehudah's and Rabbi's teacher. Yet it is surprising that Rabbi never mentioned him at all.

(n) Rambam writes that with him were his son R. Shimon; R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi; R. Yosi son of R. Yehudah; R. Yaakov of Kefar Chatya; R. Chiyya; Rav; R. Chanina bar Chama; R. Afes; Rabban Gamliel; R. Yannai; Bar Kappara; Shmuel; R. Yochanan; and R. Oshaya. These received from him. [The checked Mishneh Torah introduction lists eleven and does not include Yishmael son of Yosi, Yosi son of Yehudah, or Yaakov of Kefar Chatya.] Raavad objects that Shmuel, R. Yochanan, R. Oshaya, R. Yannai, and Bar Kappara were not of his court. Rather, Levi, R. Bisa, his son R. Chama, R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi, and R. Yosi ben Lekunya were of his court. End of quotation.

(o) The law follows him even against his father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: Asheri's rulings, Megallechin; Rashbam, Get Pashut; Hagahot Mordekhai, Ketubot. Although his father was his teacher, as in HaPoalim, Rabbi later grew wiser than he, since everywhere Rabbi's statement is taught before his father Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's. But Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam; Asheri, HaMekabbel there; Ran there and HaNizzakin; and Rif's commentary, Bnei HaIr, say the law does not follow Rabbi when he disagrees with his father. Rashba explains the places where the law does follow Rabbi against his father. If he states a law in his father's name, the law follows him: Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3. Rabbi said, “My words appear more correct than my father's”: Eruvin 32a. See Responsa Rivash, end of section 324 [on the father exception in the guardianship case]; Shelah 334a; Hagahot Mordekhai, HaMevi. The law follows him except when R. Yishmael disagrees in his father R. Yosi's name. But between R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi and Rabbi, the law follows Rabbi. See Niddah 14b. From this we learn that a rule following a particular sage includes even a disputant from an earlier generation, contrary to Tosafot Yom Tov, Negaim 1:4. Tosafot, Pesachim 48a, says this applies only where there is no further amoraic dispute. Where amoraim disagree whether it applies even against several colleagues, see Pesachim 27a; Ketubot 21a, 51a; Tosafot, Bava Batra 124b [the received text cites 122b]; Responsa Chut HaShani. Tosafot, Niddah 45b: Naarah SheNitpattatah rules like Rabbi against R. Shimon ben Elazar; Yesh Nochalin likewise rules like Rabbi against his colleague. End of quotation. Rambam, Laws of Temple Vessels, chapter 5, similarly rules like Rabbi against R. Elazar son of R. Shimon regarding an ordinary priest's belt. Beer Sheva, Tamid, Amar Lahem HaMemunneh, asks why Rambam, Laws of the Chosen House, chapter 3, rules that the menorah's lamps ran north–south, like R. Elazar son of R. Shimon against Rabbi. Although R. Elazar was superior to him in Torah, as in HaPoalim (see above), he remained within the category of colleague, and the law follows Rabbi against his colleague. More strikingly, Rashbam, Get Pashut, rules like Rabbi even when his father disagrees: although his teacher, he is not a plurality opposing him, as Rashi explains in Zeh Borer. He leaves this requiring investigation. Tosafot, Berakhot 13a; Eruvin 46b, near the end; Nazir 43a, near the end: the law follows Rabbi against one colleague, not several colleagues. R. Natan and Rabbi: the law follows R. Natan; see there. Rabbi and R. Yosi son of R. Yehudah: the law follows Rabbi.
